BLACKFOOT — The city of Blackfoot will implement water use restrictions from May 1 through Oct. 1 for all residents and businesses connected to the city water system, Mayor Scott Stufflebeam announced during this week's Blackfoot City Council meeting.

The reason is simple: it's shaping up to be a dry year.

Stufflebeam said updates received April 3 paint a concerning picture — peak flow of the Snake River is predicted to drop to 70% this summer, Island Park Reservoir sits at just 65% of normal and snowpack is estimated at 59% of normal. Regional reservoirs tell a similar story. According to the Bureau of Reclamation, American Falls Reservoir is at 83% capacity, Ririe Reservoir at 72% and Palisades Reservoir at just 61%.

"It is going to be a hard water year," said Water Superintendent Princton Lee. "I think most people realize we didn't have much of a winter."

The rules are straightforward. Residents and businesses with addresses ending in an even number may only water lawns and landscaping on even-numbered days. Those with odd-numbered addresses are restricted to odd-numbered days.

"No one is allowed to water on the 31st day of the month," Lee said.

The city also recommends watering during low-evaporation hours — before 10 a.m. or after 6 p.m.

Beyond the restrictions, Lee outlined several steps residents can take to reduce their overall water usage.

"You can reduce lawn space by adding flowerbeds using mulch, which will help retain water," he said. "There are a lot of xeriscaping options that can help reduce water usage as well."

Xeriscaping uses drought-tolerant native plants, efficient irrigation and mulching to create landscapes requiring significantly less water. For those unwilling to part with their lawn, Lee offered a simpler tip.

"Leaving your grass a little longer helps to keep the moisture in the ground," he said.

Lee said this could be an isolated dry year — but he's not counting on it. He noted that drier conditions have been trending geographically northward for several years.

"Sometimes people think of conservation as a dirty word, but it just comes down to using less of a valuable resource," he said. "It comes down to a habit change. It's possible that this could be the way it is going to be, and we have to adjust because the climate is adjusting."
